title: How do we order eight tenth numbers?
description: Eight number cards are written as counts of tenths so that they can be put in order from the smallest to the biggest. Keeko doubts the last card and thinks the card with the biggest count of tenths is the biggest number.
teaching_notes: One idea: numbers are compared by counting the same part, so every card is changed to a count of tenths first. Watch for students who pick the card with the biggest-looking top number.

video_script.why: The child can change a length to a count of tenths and now uses that count to compare eight numbers.
video_script.substitution: Change every number to a count of tenths, then put the counts in order.
video_script.anchor: Eight number cards written as units and tenths or as tenths, lined up in a row
video_script.wrong_answer: one hundred thirty tenths is the biggest
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko picks 130/10 as the biggest because 130 is the biggest-looking number, but 130 tenths is only 13 units, which is less than 13 1/10.
video_script.payoff_line: The smallest is four tenths, then nine tenths, then one and seven tenths

final_answer.spoken: four tenths, nine tenths, one and seven tenths, six and seven tenths, seven and six tenths, ten and five tenths, one hundred thirty tenths, thirteen and one tenth

maths_rules: Slip: 130 looks biggest, but 130 tenths is 13 units and 131 tenths is 13 1/10.
video_script.design: One idea: numbers are compared once they count the same part, so every number is changed to a count of tenths. Assumes the child can change units and tenths into tenths. Wrong idea: the biggest-looking top number is the biggest. The eight cards stay all video.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; eight number cards are laid in a row in the anchor band: 9/10, 1 7/10, 130/10, 13 1/10, 10 5/10, 7 6/10, 6 7/10, 4/10

marks.cards: the eight cards appear in a row

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='cards'/>Eight number cards lie on the board.
<bookmark mark='a'/>The first two say nine tenths, and one and seven tenths.
<bookmark mark='b'/>The next two say one hundred thirty tenths, and thirteen and one tenth.
<bookmark mark='c'/>The rest say ten and five tenths, seven and six tenths, six and seven tenths, four tenths.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>In what order do they go from smallest to biggest?

beats.on_screen: the eight cards stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a unit bar cut into 10 parts, each labelled 1/10; the words same part, then count appear under it

marks.part: the unit bar is cut into 10 parts, each labelled 1/10
marks.count: the words same part, then count appear under the bar

narration: <bookmark mark='part'/>We can compare numbers when they count the same part.
<bookmark mark='count'/>Here the part is one tenth. We write every card as a count of tenths.

marks.first: the first four cards are written
marks.last: the last four cards are written

narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Given, eight cards. Nine tenths, one and seven tenths, one hundred thirty tenths, and thirteen and one tenth.
<bookmark mark='last'/>Then ten and five tenths, seven and six tenths, six and seven tenths, and four tenths.

beats.on_screen: To find: the cards in order, smallest to biggest

marks.find: the words smallest to biggest are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to put the cards in order, from smallest to biggest.

marks.one: the five cards with a whole number are lined up

narration: <bookmark mark='one'/>Step one, change the cards that have a whole number into tenths.
<bookmark mark='a'/>Ten tenths make one unit, so one and seven tenths is seventeen tenths.
<bookmark mark='b'/>Six and seven tenths is sixty seven tenths. Seven and six tenths is seventy six tenths.
<bookmark mark='c'/>Ten and five tenths is one hundred five tenths. Thirteen and one tenth is one hundred thirty one tenths.

marks.two: the three cards that are already tenths are marked
marks.all: all eight counts are written in a row

narration: <bookmark mark='two'/>Step two, the other three cards already count tenths. They are nine tenths, one hundred thirty tenths, and four tenths.
<bookmark mark='all'/>All eight cards are now counts of the same part.

marks.three: the counts slide into a new row

narration: <bookmark mark='three'/>Step three, put the counts in order.
<bookmark mark='small'/>Four, nine, seventeen, sixty seven, and seventy six.
<bookmark mark='big'/>Then one hundred five, one hundred thirty, and one hundred thirty one.

marks.ans: each count changes back to its card and the row is boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The smallest is four tenths, then nine tenths, then one and seven tenths.
<bookmark mark='rest'/>After them come six and seven tenths, seven and six tenths, and ten and five tenths.
<bookmark mark='last'/>The last two are one hundred thirty tenths, and thirteen and one tenth.
<bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble shows 130/10 is the biggest; below it 130 tenths is 13 units and 131 tenths is 13 1/10; the bubble is struck through in the warning colour

marks.doubt: the bubble 130/10 is the biggest appears
marks.fix: the bubble is struck through and 131 tenths is placed after 130 tenths

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks one hundred thirty tenths is the biggest, because one hundred thirty looks like a big number.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But one hundred thirty one tenths has one more tenth. Thirteen and one tenth is the biggest card.
